doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: Jazz and classical worlds at Eastman
summary: He praises the classical trumpet teacher Jim Thompson and argues for classical foundations in jazz players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do the jazz students at Eastman, even the faculty, do you feel like more of a clannish clique at Eastman? Are you separate from the classical world or not?

No. I’m going to say that’s one thing I love about Eastman is generally speaking no. The other trumpet teacher there is one of the — the classical trumpet teacher there, the main guy, is one of the best trumpet players I’ve ever heard in my life. His name is Jim Thompson. He is so respectful of the jazz. Now that’s not always the case in schools. But Jim is so respectful to me and of the jazz thing. And he’s not a jazz player whatsoever. So I think in some schools it is an issue. It definitely is. Like oh you can’t play in the big band because you have a recital this semester, and that kind of stuff. Jim would never say that. He couldn’t care less.

Oh sure. And sometimes the jazz guys are a little bit better versed at playing in a brass quintet than the brass quintet guys are, because of style more than anything. So that’s something that we work on. And I give studio classes with his students all the time. Because he’s of the opinion that in the future, and I agree with him, in the future a symphonic trumpet section might consist of a principal player and then a second player, and then a guy that can play lead on some pop stuff, and then a guy that can stand up and play changes and not sound silly, as well as be a good fourth trumpet player in a symphony. I mean that’s smart.
Because students still do the classical path first.

Sure. Especially on certain instruments like trumpet. I think that’s important. Because you need to be a good classical player to be a good jazz player. Otherwise that horn’s going to get in your way. Now other instruments not so much. Drummers don’t have to be great mallet players or guitar players might not need to have classical chops necessarily. I don’t know. I don’t want to speak for them. Bass players I think need to have good arco/bowing technique. They need to have good classical technique. And it’s tried and true technique. John Clayton’s a beautiful classical player. Jeff Campbell, the jazz teacher at Eastman, he’s in the RPO. He’s a beautiful player. And you can hear it in his pitch and his dexterity and articulation. You can hear that he’s a really great bass player. And he got that from being a good classical player. So yeah, I think we need to go through that. And that’s another thing I like about Eastman is that the kids have to pass — like the piano players, they have to pass some classical barriers. They just do. That’s just part of it. So that’s the thing I love about it. Now I’m sure there are faculty at Eastman that, “ah, they’re jazzers.” But generally, and the administration is incredibly supportive of the jazz department. So that’s one thing I actually like about it, more so than other schools.
